title: 6 Best Gas Generators (2026): Picks by Household and Fuel Plan
metaDescription: The Generac GP8000E leads 6 gas generators; an 8,000-watt open frame at half load burns roughly 14 to 19 gallons a day, so each pick comes with a fuel plan.
intro:
The Generac GP8000E is the best gas generator for most homes: 8,000 running and 10,000 starting watts, enough for a 240V well pump plus essentials through a transfer switch. What you need to run, and how much gasoline you can store, changes the answer. This guide ranks six gasoline generators, works out fuel burn, and covers storage, hookup and carbon monoxide safety.

No outage option buys more power per dollar than a gasoline generator, but it expects discipline in return: a realistic fuel plan, stabilized storage, a monthly test run, a proper transfer switch, and a parking spot well away from the house. Handle those and a gas portable is the best-value backup most homes can buy.
quickAnswer: the Generac GP8000E Electric-Start Portable is our #1 pick (top gasoline pick). The first gasoline portable to consider for a house with a well, a sump or a history of long outages.
picksHeading: The 6 Best Gas Generators in 2026, Ranked

picks.body: The GP8000E lands on the size most houses really need from a gasoline portable. Generac rates it at 8,000 running and 10,000 starting watts, which is enough to start a 240V well pump while a refrigerator, freezer, furnace blower and lights stay on, as long as it feeds the house through a transfer switch or interlock. Electric start runs off an onboard battery, with a recoil cord as a fallback, and COsense stops the engine if carbon monoxide builds up around it. A steel cradle and never-flat tires suit a machine that lives in a shed and gets hauled across a soggy yard. The tank holds roughly 8 gallons and Generac lists a long run time at half load, but this is a conventional fixed-speed engine, so it will not match an inverter's economy at light loads. Owners commonly praise how reliably it starts when maintained, and they mention the noise. Expect roughly $1,000 to $1,300 at the time of writing.
pros: 8,000 running watts handles a 240V well pump plus the essentials
Electric start, with a pull cord as backup
120/240V locking outlet for a transfer switch
cons: Fixed-speed engine keeps burning fuel steadily even at light load

picks.body: The WGen9500 delivers a lot of gasoline generator for its price. Westinghouse rates it at 9,500 running and 12,500 starting watts, one step above the 8,000-watt class, which leaves room for a window air conditioner or a bigger well pump on top of the usual essentials. Key-fob remote start is genuinely handy in bad weather, and the outlet panel carries both a 30-amp and a 50-amp 120/240V locking outlet, so it can feed either common size of transfer switch or inlet. The 6.6-gallon tank has a fuel gauge, and Westinghouse lists a long run time at moderate load. It is heavy enough that you will lean on the wheels and handle, and at high loads it goes through gasoline quickly. Newer production adds a carbon monoxide sensor; check that the unit you buy has it. Expect roughly $1,100 to $1,500 at the time of writing.
pros: 9,500 running watts for what many 8,000W units cost
Remote start from a key fob
Long Westinghouse warranty and US-based support

picks.body: When gasoline is hard to find during your outages, the iGen4500 is the most fuel-savvy generator on this list. Being an inverter, it throttles its engine down as demand falls, so a refrigerator, freezer, furnace blower and lights drawing a few hundred to 2,000 watts use far less fuel than the same loads on an open-frame machine. Westinghouse rates it at 3,700 running and 4,500 starting watts on a 3.4-gallon tank and lists long run times at light load. It is also much quieter, which helps with neighbors and with sleep. Electric and remote start, a fuel and run-time display, and clean output for electronics complete the package. The limits: it is 120V only, so it cannot run a 240V well pump, and it lacks the output for central air. For a house with gas heat and a basement, it covers the essentials on a fraction of the gasoline. Expect roughly $1,000 to $1,300 at the time of writing.
pros: Inverter efficiency makes gasoline last longer at light loads
Display shows the run time left
cons: Cannot match open-frame output for whole-house essentials

picks.body: Firman's P08004 is a plain, no-frills way into the 8,000-watt class. On gasoline it is rated at 8,000 running and 10,000 starting watts, the same headline numbers as the GP8000E, and its 120/240V output can feed a transfer switch or interlock. That handles a well pump or sump pump plus a refrigerator, freezer, furnace blower and lights in a typical house. The frame and wheels are made for rough handling, and the controls are simple. The lower price mostly costs you on support: Firman's service network is thinner than Generac's or Westinghouse's, and the feature list is shorter. Owners commonly report that it starts and runs well when it gets fresh, stabilized fuel and regular exercise. Carbon monoxide shutoff and start type vary by version, so check the specific listing. Expect roughly $800 to $1,100 at the time of writing.
pros: 8,000 running watts for less than most name brands charge
Tough steel frame and wheel kit
cons: Thinner service network than Generac or Westinghouse

picks.body: Plenty of gas generator buyers do not need 8,000 watts. If an outage means keeping a refrigerator, lights, internet and phones going, or a gas furnace blower, the EU2200i does it on remarkably little fuel. Honda rates it at 1,800 running and 2,200 starting watts, with a listed run time of about 3.2 hours at full rated load and about 8.1 hours at a quarter load on its 0.95-gallon tank. At that rate, a few gallons of stabilized gasoline covers a long stretch of outage. It weighs about 47 pounds, runs quietly, and its CO-MINDER system shuts the engine down if carbon monoxide collects nearby. You can parallel it with a second unit if you need more power later. You pay more than for similar-spec rivals, mostly for the engine's reputation and Honda's dealer network. Expect roughly $1,100 to $1,300 at the time of writing.
pros: Honda engine with an outstanding reliability record
Runs up to about 8 hours at quarter load on under a gallon

picks.body: The XP12000E is the gasoline-only version of DuroMax's large portable, rated at 9,500 running and 12,000 starting watts. In some cases that is enough for a modest central air conditioner, particularly with a soft-start kit, or for a big share of a house with gas heat and a gas water heater. A 50-amp 120/240V outlet suits a larger transfer switch or panel interlock. Power comes from a 457cc engine with electric start, and the alternator uses copper windings. All that output brings weight of well over 200 pounds, noise, and fuel burn that can reach many gallons a day under heavy load. If you are weighing one, run the fuel math first and compare its total cost with a small standby generator on natural gas; for some homes the standby comes out ahead once fuel and labor are counted. Expect roughly $1,100 to $1,500 at the time of writing.
cons: Burns a lot of fuel at high load

sections.heading: Does Gas Generator Mean Gasoline or Natural Gas?
sections.body:
Usually it means gasoline. When people shop for a gas generator, they almost always mean a portable machine with its own tank that you fill from a can. Natural gas generators do exist, but nearly all of them are permanently installed standby units piped into the home's gas line. The two are separate purchases, with different prices, installation and safety considerations.

### What does a gasoline portable trade away?

This guide is about gasoline portables. They cost a fraction of what a standby unit does, need no installation beyond a transfer switch or interlock, and can be rolled to wherever you need power. The trade is that you handle the fuel, the starting, the connection and the placement yourself in every outage.

### Where do natural gas standby units fit?

If you would rather have a machine that starts by itself and runs for days off a utility gas line, our [Generac cost guide](/generac-generator-cost/) breaks down what a natural gas standby system really costs once installed, and our [home generator rankings](/best-home-generator-for-power-outages/) set standby, gasoline, dual fuel and battery options side by side.

### Is there a middle ground?

Yes. Dual fuel portables run on gasoline or propane, and tri-fuel models add natural gas through a quick-connect. They give up a little output on the gaseous fuels in exchange for far easier long-term fuel storage, and they deserve a look if the fuel headaches described below worry you. Our [dual fuel generator guide](/best-dual-fuel-generator/) ranks them.

sections.heading: What Size Gas Generator Do You Need for a House?
sections.body:
A house on city water with gas heat and no basement typically needs 2,000 to 3,500 running watts, while a house with a private well usually lands in the 8,000-watt class or above. The well pump, the sump and any air conditioning decide which side of that line you fall on.

### How do you build a load list?

List what has to run, not what would be nice to have. For most homes that is the refrigerator, freezer, lights, internet, a gas furnace blower in winter, a sump pump if there is a basement, and a well pump if the house is not on city water. Read each appliance's running watts from its data plate, add them up, then add the single biggest starting surge on top.

| House situation | Typical running watts needed | Gas generator class |
| --- | --- | --- |
| City water, gas heat, no basement | 2,000-3,500W | 2,200-4,500W inverter |
| City water, gas heat, basement sump | 3,500-5,500W | 4,500W inverter to 8,000W open frame |
| Private well, gas heat, sump | 5,500-7,500W including pump start | 8,000-9,500W open frame with 240V |
| Essentials plus window AC or two | 7,000-9,000W | 9,500W open frame |
| Central AC and most of the house | 12,000W and up | Standby, or a very large portable with soft start |

### Why is a 240V well pump the dividing line?

A 240-volt well pump needs a generator with a 120/240V outlet, usually an L14-30 or a 14-50, connected through a transfer switch or interlock. Its starting surge can run two to three times its running draw. Together those two facts push most houses with a well into the 8,000-watt class or higher. Our [well pump generator guide](/best-generator-for-well-pump/) covers that case in detail.

### How much headroom should you leave?

Plan to use no more than about 75 to 80 percent of the running rating. A generator held at 90 percent of its rating for days on end runs hot, loud and thirsty, and the voltage sags that come with it are hard on motors. If your list adds up to 6,000 watts, an 8,000-watt unit is the right size; a 6,500-watt unit is not.

### Can a gas generator be too big?

Yes. A 9,500-watt generator feeding 2,000 watts of load burns almost as much fuel per hour as it does at half load. When your essentials are modest, a mid-size inverter or a smaller open frame runs far longer on the same can of gasoline. For homes where 4,500 watts is plenty, our [small generator picks](/best-small-generator-for-home/) are the better starting point.

sections.heading: How Much Gas Does a Generator Use per Day?
sections.body:
An 8,000-watt open frame burning about 0.7 gallons an hour uses roughly 17 gallons in a day of nonstop running, and three days takes more than 50 gallons. Smaller inverters use a fraction of that, and running in cycles can cut any of these totals by half or more.

Typical Gasoline Consumption

0.1-0.3 gal/hr

2,200W inverter, light load

0.3-0.5 gal/hr

4,500W inverter, moderate load

0.6-0.8 gal/hr

8,000W open frame, half load

0.8-1.2 gal/hr

9,500W+ open frame, heavy load

### Why do fuel plans fall apart?

Fuel is where most gas generator plans break down. Makers list run time at 25 or 50 percent load, which is fair, but owners routinely underestimate how many hours they will run and overestimate how easy fuel will be to buy during a regional outage. Gas stations need electricity to pump, and the few that have it draw long lines.

The consumption figures above are typical ranges, not specifications, so check the manual for your model. At around 0.7 gallons an hour, three days of round-the-clock running needs more gasoline than most people can store safely or legally at home.

### How does cycling cut fuel use?

Run in cycles. A refrigerator and freezer hold their cold for hours once chilled, a sump pit can usually be pumped down and left for a while in most storms, and a house with gas heat loses warmth slowly. Two hours on followed by three or four hours off can cut fuel use by half or more. Many owners pair this routine with a [battery power station](/best-portable-power-station/) that carries the router, phones and a few lights while the generator rests.

### How do you do the math before buying?

Multiply your realistic running hours per day by the gallons per hour at your expected load, then multiply by the number of days your typical long outage lasts. If the answer is uncomfortably large, pick an inverter, pick dual fuel, or plan to cycle.

sections.heading: How Do You Store Gasoline for a Generator?
sections.body:
Store it stabilized, in approved sealed cans, outside the living space, and rotate it every few months. Pump gasoline was never meant for long-term storage, and treating it like an emergency supply that keeps forever is how generators end up refusing to start.

### Why does gasoline go bad?

Its lighter compounds evaporate, it oxidizes into gums and varnish, and the ethanol in most blends pulls moisture out of the air. Left untreated, it can start causing small-engine starting problems within a month or two, and after several months it can leave deposits that only a carburetor cleaning will clear.

### How should you use fuel stabilizer?

Add stabilizer every time you fill a storage can, not only before the generator is put away for winter. Labels commonly claim one to two years of protection, but rotation is still the better habit: pour stored gasoline into your car every few months and refill the cans with fresh, stabilized fuel. Where you can buy ethanol-free gasoline, it stores better and is gentler on small engines.

### Where should the cans live?

Use approved, tightly sealed containers, preferably with spill-proof spouts, and keep them out of the living space: a detached shed or garage, away from water heaters, furnaces, dryers and anything else with a flame or spark, and out of direct sun. Local fire codes often cap how much gasoline you can keep at home, commonly at around 25 gallons in a residential garage, so look up your local rule before you stockpile. Set the cans on a shelf or floor away from where children play, and label each one with the date it was filled.

### How do you refuel safely?

Turn the engine off and let it cool for several minutes before adding fuel. Gasoline spilled on a hot muffler or exhaust is one of the most common ways generators start fires.

STORAGE RULE OF THUMB

Stabilize every can, rotate every season.

Think of stored gasoline as milk with a long date: fine for a while, a little worse every month. Add stabilizer when you fill the can, write the date on it, burn it in your car within a few months, and refill. The generator starts when you need it, and you never have to pour out a can of varnish.

sections.heading: Is Gasoline Better Than Propane or Natural Gas for a Generator?
sections.body:
Gasoline gives the most power per gallon and full rated output, but it is the hardest of the three to store. Propane keeps for years without breaking down and comes in standard cylinders sold almost everywhere. Natural gas never needs storing, but it only works through a fixed connection, usually on a standby unit.

| Fuel | Shelf life | Output vs gasoline | Main drawback |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gasoline | Months, longer with stabilizer | Full rated output | Goes stale; hard to buy in outages |
| Propane | Indefinite in a sound tank | Roughly 10 percent less | More fuel volume per hour; cylinders can struggle in deep cold |
| Natural gas | No storage needed | Often 10 to 20 percent less | Requires a gas line and fixed installation |

### Why is propane the backup worth planning around?

For anyone running a gasoline portable, propane is the most useful second fuel to consider. A dual fuel generator lets you burn stabilized gasoline first and then switch to a row of 20-pound cylinders once the cans are empty. Propane also ends the stale-fuel carburetor problem, because the carburetor holds no liquid fuel while running on it.

### When does gasoline-only still make sense?

Gasoline remains the right call for many households. It has the highest energy density of the three, you can rotate it through the family car, and gasoline-only units tend to be a little cheaper and simpler. The condition is that fuel planning becomes part of the purchase rather than an afterthought.

sections.heading: Should You Buy an Open-Frame or Inverter Gas Generator?
sections.body:
Buy an open frame if you need 240 volts for a well pump, a large sump or a window air conditioner, and an inverter if your loads are a refrigerator, furnace blower and lights. The inverter can use half the gasoline over an outage; the open frame brings the surge and voltage bigger loads demand.

### How does an open-frame generator work?

Open-frame generators hold a fixed engine speed to produce 60-hertz power directly. They cost less per watt and come in large sizes with 240V outlets, which is why they dominate the 8,000-watt-and-up class. They are also louder, and they burn fuel at a fairly steady rate regardless of load.

### What does an inverter do differently?

Inverter generators change engine speed to match demand and build clean 60-hertz power electronically. They are quieter, much more efficient at light loads, and safer for electronics. Most are 120V only and stop at around 4,500 watts, though a handful of larger inverter models exist at higher prices. Our [inverter generator guide](/best-inverter-generator/) compares them.

### Which one saves more gasoline?

In a household where the generator mostly runs a refrigerator, furnace blower and lights, an inverter can burn half the gasoline an open frame would over the same outage. In a house with a well pump, a larger sump pump or a window air conditioner, the open frame's 240V output and surge capacity are what the job requires.

### Is there a practical compromise?

For some homes, yes: own a mid-size inverter for ordinary outages and borrow or rent more capacity for the rare extreme event, or pair an open frame with a battery station so the engine only runs part of the day. Either approach shrinks the amount of fuel you need to keep on hand.

sections.heading: Which Gas Generator Features Are Worth Paying For?
sections.body:
Automatic carbon monoxide shutoff comes first, then electric start and a 120/240V outlet that matches your inlet. After those, an hour meter, a fuel gauge, solid wheels and the right emissions certification are worth checking before you buy.

### Automatic CO shutoff

Make **automatic CO shutoff** the first feature you insist on. It adds little to the price, it is now common across the major brands, and it targets the way generators actually kill people. Look for ANSI/PGMA G300 or UL 2201 on the box or the spec sheet.

### Electric start

**Electric start** matters more than it seems in the store. Yanking a recoil cord on a 450cc engine in freezing rain is hard work, and for older owners it can decide whether the generator gets used at all. Remote start fobs are a pleasant extra, but they do not change the placement rules: the generator still sits 20 feet or more from the house. Keep the pull cord as a backup and keep the starting battery charged.

### The right outlet, meter, gauge and wheels

**A 120/240V outlet that matches your inlet** is essential for a house with a well pump or a transfer switch. An **hour meter** makes oil-change intervals easy to keep track of, and a **fuel gauge** saves you from opening a hot tank to check the level. Never-flat tires and a folding handle earn their keep on anything heavier than about 150 pounds.

### Emissions certification and warranty

Check the emissions certification as well. California and some other states allow only CARB-compliant small engines to be sold, and most national brands now ship CARB versions; EPA certification is standard. Finally, compare warranties. Three years of residential coverage is common among the major brands, and a local service dealer is worth more than an extra year printed on paper.

sections.heading: How Do You Connect a Gas Generator to Your House Safely?
sections.body:
Through a **manual transfer switch** or a listed **panel interlock kit**, each fed by an outdoor power inlet and installed by a licensed electrician with a permit. Those are the only safe and legal ways to run hardwired loads such as the furnace, the well pump or a sump pump on its own circuit, which is where a large gasoline portable earns its keep. Never backfeed the house without one.

BACKFEED WARNING

No dryer-outlet shortcuts, ever.

Plugging a generator into a dryer or wall receptacle with a double-male cord sends power backward through your panel and onto the utility lines, where transformers step it up to thousands of volts and put line workers and neighbors at risk. It bypasses the protection built into your home, can wreck the generator when grid power returns, violates the National Electrical Code and is illegal in most jurisdictions.

### Which inlet matches your generator?

Size the inlet to the generator's largest outlet. Most portables from 7,000 to 9,500 watts carry an L14-30 30-amp 120/240V locking outlet, and many bigger units add a 14-50 50-amp outlet. A 30-amp connection delivers up to about 7,200 watts; if your generator can supply more and your load list needs it, a 50-amp inlet puts the extra capacity to use.

### What does a transfer switch or interlock cost?

A manual transfer switch, usually covering six to ten selected circuits, commonly runs $800 to $1,800 installed, including the inlet and permit. An interlock kit is often cheaper, roughly $500 to $1,200 installed, and lets you pick any circuit, but you have to manage the load yourself so the generator is not overloaded. Either costs far less than a fire or an injury. Our [transfer switch guide](/best-generator-transfer-switch/) compares the options.

### What cord and GFCI issues come up?

Run a properly rated generator cord from the unit to the inlet, as short as the 20-foot-plus placement rule allows, and route it so nobody trips over it. Some newer generators have GFCI protection that can trip when connected to a house panel because of the way neutral and ground are bonded; your electrician can resolve that correctly. A circuit breaker finder speeds up labeling the circuits you want to include.

sections.heading: Where Should a Gas Generator Sit to Avoid Carbon Monoxide?
sections.body:
Outdoors only, at least 20 feet from the house, with the exhaust pointed away from doors, windows, vents and your neighbors' homes. Gasoline generators produce large amounts of carbon monoxide, an odorless, colorless gas that kills people every storm season, often while they sleep, and most of those deaths involve generators run in garages, basements or right beside the house.

### Where should it never run?

Never in a garage, even with the door open. Never in a basement, crawlspace, carport or shed, and never on a roofed porch next to the house. Open doors and fans do not make an enclosed space safe.

### Which alarms and shutoffs help?

Install CO alarms that keep working without grid power, either battery-only or with battery backup, on every level and near the bedrooms, and test them before storm season. Choose a generator with automatic CO shutoff, sold under names such as COsense, CO-MINDER and CO Shield and certified to ANSI/PGMA G300 or UL 2201; it kills the engine when carbon monoxide builds up around it. Treat it as a safety net, never as permission to move the generator closer.

### How do you run it in rain or snow?

Use a generator tent or ventilated cover made for use while the engine runs, or a freestanding canopy out in the open. Weather is never a reason to bring the generator into a garage or under the eaves.

### What are the warning signs?

A headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion in anyone in the house, or a sounding CO alarm, means everyone goes outside into fresh air immediately. Call 911 once you are out.

THE 20-FOOT RULE

Outside, 20 feet out, exhaust aimed away.

No garage, basement, carport, shed or covered porch, whatever the weather. Battery-backed CO alarms inside on every level, and a CO shutoff on the generator as a second layer, never a first.

sections.heading: How Do You Keep a Gas Generator Ready to Start?
sections.body:
Run it monthly under load, store it the way the manual says, and keep the oil and starting battery fresh. Most gas generators that let their owners down in an outage fail at the pull cord or the key switch, not under load, and the cause is almost always stale fuel, a dead battery or old oil.

### Run it monthly with a real load

Once a month, start the generator and let it run for 15 to 30 minutes with something plugged in, such as a space heater or a shop light. That pulls fresh fuel through the carburetor, charges the starting battery on models that do so, and exposes problems while there is still time to fix them calmly.

### Pick a storage approach and stick to it

Either keep the tank full of stabilized fuel, which limits air space and condensation, or close the fuel valve and run the carburetor dry before storing the machine. Manufacturers disagree about which is better, so follow your manual. What you should never do is leave untreated gasoline sitting in the carburetor for months.

### Change the oil on schedule and keep the battery charged

A new engine needs an early first oil change, often after a few hours of break-in, and then regular changes based on run hours. During a long outage, check the oil every day, because a multi-day run can reach the service interval quickly. On electric-start units, keep the battery on a maintainer if the generator does not charge it between uses, and replace it every few years.

mistakes.title: Counting on buying fuel during the outage
mistakes.body: In a regional outage, gas stations close, and the few that can still pump draw long lines. Owners who plan to buy fuel as they go often run dry by day two. Keep enough stabilized gasoline for your realistic first two or three days, rotate it, and cycle the generator so every gallon goes further.

mistakes.title: Buying the biggest generator on the shelf
mistakes.body: A 12,000-watt generator running only a fridge and lights burns gasoline nearly as fast as it would at half load, and it is far harder to move and store. Size to your real load list plus about 20 to 25 percent headroom. For modest loads, a mid-size inverter does the same job on much less fuel.

mistakes.title: Refueling a hot engine
mistakes.body: Pouring gasoline into a running or just-stopped generator risks splashing it onto a hot muffler, where it can ignite. Switch the engine off, give it several minutes to cool, refuel carefully with a spill-proof spout, wipe up any drips, and only then restart. Keep a fire extinguisher rated for flammable liquids within reach.

mistakes.title: Storing it with fuel that goes stale
mistakes.body: The fresh gasoline in your tank today is stale gasoline a few months from now. A generator left through the off-season with untreated fuel often refuses to start in the first storm. Add stabilizer to every can when you fill it, run the unit under load once a month, and follow the manual's long-term storage steps.

mistakes.title: Backfeeding through a dryer outlet
mistakes.body: Some owners reach the panel by plugging a generator into a dryer receptacle with a homemade double-male cord. That pushes power onto the utility lines, where it can kill line workers, and it can start fires and wreck the generator when grid power returns. Have an electrician install a transfer switch or interlock with an inlet instead.

faqs.q: How many gallons of gas does a generator use in a day?
faqs.a: That comes down to size and load. Over 24 hours, a 2,200-watt inverter at light load may burn 2 to 4 gallons, a 4,500-watt inverter roughly 6 to 10, and an 8,000-watt open frame at half load about 14 to 19. Cycling the generator, a couple of hours on and a few hours off, can cut those totals by half or more.

faqs.q: How long can gasoline sit in a generator before it goes bad?
faqs.a: Untreated gasoline, especially an ethanol blend, can cause small-engine starting trouble within a month or two. Stabilizer added while the fuel is still fresh stretches that, and labels commonly claim one to two years. The safer habit is to rotate stored fuel every few months, run the generator once a month, and follow the owner's manual for storage.

faqs.q: Can I run a gas generator all night?
faqs.a: Yes, provided it sits outdoors at least 20 feet from the house with the exhaust aimed away, has enough fuel, and battery-powered CO alarms are working inside. Never refuel it while it runs. Many owners shut it down overnight once the fridge and freezer are cold, or hand overnight loads to a battery station, which saves fuel and keeps neighbors happy.

faqs.q: Is gasoline or dual fuel better for home backup?
faqs.a: For outage backup, dual fuel usually comes out ahead, because propane keeps indefinitely and gives you a second fuel when gasoline runs short. Expect roughly 10 percent less output on propane. Gasoline-only models are simpler and sometimes cheaper. If you will reliably rotate stabilized gasoline, either type works; if you will not, dual fuel is more forgiving.

faqs.q: What size gas generator runs a whole house?
faqs.a: True whole-house coverage, including central air, an electric water heater or electric cooking, usually takes 15,000 to 25,000 watts or more, which is standby territory. A large portable rated at 9,500 to 12,000 running watts can carry most of a gas-heated house through a transfer switch, especially when you manage loads. Households that only need essentials need far less.

faqs.q: How much gasoline can I legally store at home?
faqs.a: Local fire codes set the limit, and it varies. Many residential codes allow around 25 gallons in approved containers in a garage or shed, while some places are stricter or ban storage in attached garages. Ask your local fire department, and keep fuel out of the living space and away from ignition sources, in approved, sealed cans.

faqs.q: Do gas generators need a transfer switch?
faqs.a: Not when you only run extension cords from the generator to individual appliances. Powering hardwired loads such as a furnace, well pump or panel circuits requires a manual transfer switch or a listed interlock kit with an inlet, installed by a licensed electrician under a permit. Plugging the generator into a wall or dryer outlet instead is dangerous and illegal.

bottomLine:
For most houses that want gasoline backup, the Generac GP8000E is the one to buy: enough 240-volt output for a well or sump plus the essentials, electric start, CO shutoff and broad service support. The Westinghouse WGen9500 is the value step up in watts, and the iGen4500 is the smart pick when fuel supply and noise count for more than raw output.

Whichever you choose, plan the fuel before the storm, stabilize and rotate it, run the generator every month, connect it only through a transfer switch or interlock, and park it outdoors well away from the house with CO alarms working inside. Those habits are what turn a gas generator into a safe, dependable backup instead of a hazard.
